svg.title: Four layers of path control, and the case where the metric cannot express the intent
svg.desc: Four stacked layers, each with the question it answers and the tool it uses. Layer one, which prefixes exist, answered by filtering and summarization. Layer two, which path is preferred, answered by metric tuning, offset lists, or policy-based routing. Layer three, which path is propagated, answered by route maps and BGP attributes. Layer four, what happens when the preferred path fails, answered by redundancy design and fast reroute. A lower panel shows a case where equal cost hides a ten to one capacity difference: a one gigabit link and a ten gigabit link between the same two routers both compute cost 1 under the default reference bandwidth, so the network load-shares when it should prefer the faster link. Three fixes are listed: change the reference bandwidth, set an explicit interface cost, or accept the hash-based load sharing deliberately and document it.
svg.text: Path control has four layers, and they answer four different questions
Most “the path is wrong” tickets are answered at layer 1 — the prefix should not have been there at all
Layer 1 · Which prefixes exist
Filtering, summarization, default-originate.
The cheapest layer: remove the choice instead of tuning it.
Layer 2 · Which path is preferred
Metric, reference bandwidth, offset lists, PBR.
Local decision, visible in the routing table.
Layer 3 · Which path is propagated
Route maps, BGP attributes, communities.
This is where policy leaves one domain and enters another.
Layer 4 · What happens when it fails
Redundancy, fast reroute, backup paths.
Truth is revealed here, not in the primary path design.
WHEN THE METRIC CANNOT EXPRESS THE INTENT
R1
R2
10G link
1G link
Default reference 100 Mbps: both links cost 1.
The network load-shares 50/50 over a 10:1 capacity gap,
so half the traffic takes the wrong link and nothing reports it.
THREE HONEST FIXES
1. Raise the reference bandwidth so the ratio survives: 1G becomes 100, 10G becomes 10.
2. Set an explicit interface cost where the formula cannot be trusted, and document why.
3. Accept the load sharing on purpose: if the hash distributes flows anyway, say so in the design.
What is not a fix: assuming the protocol noticed the speed difference.
The asymmetry check
Cost is computed locally, so R1 and R2 can disagree. Always verify the
cost on both ends of a link, never from one router's output alone.
Order of attack: before touching a metric, ask whether the prefix should be reachable by that path at all. Layer 1 solves most path problems
without creating a second one, and it leaves a network that a new engineer can still read from the routing table.
Test that proves layer 4: shut the preferred link during a maintenance window and measure recovery. A path design that was never failed over is a hypothesis, not a design.
